coherence.reasons: Both follow the same sound chain: bridge, why the draft plan fails, sized levers, first moves, asks. Y is leaner and its executive summary maps cleanly to its pages. But Y's headline ("3% is reachable", ~3.2%) is sized at FY2025 scale and leaves out the known 2027 wage step. Its own risk page puts that step at up to $6.7M, which would take the base plan to about 2.7%, so the headline only holds with contingency levers that are outside the base plan. X builds the wage step and delivery-rate rise into the baseline, so its governing thought (2.6% on firm levers, second wave to 3.0%) matches its bridge, lever table, sensitivities and asks. X has small blemishes: some titles say "reaches 3.0%" while firm levers give 2.6%, and the target is quoted as $45M, $43.3M and $42–43M on different pages. On balance X's numbers hang together slightly better.

judgment.reasons: Both recommend an R1-type plan with a targeted labour reallocation in place of the 8% cut, delivery repricing, a promotion reset, shrink, private label and six store exits. X weighs more alternatives: the management draft, click-and-collect only as an explicit fallback needing the owners' consent, deeper promotions against ValuMart, and exiting all nine stores now. X also sizes the promotion-versus-traffic trade-off (25% lost-volume haircut, 50% in the sensitivity), where Y leaves the ValuMart traffic risk unsized. X is candid that firm levers reach only 2.6% and sets a mid-FY2027 checkpoint to trigger the second wave. Y claims 3.2% by treating the scheduled wage rise as a risk. It then closes the gap with stretch contingencies (shrink to 2.1%, promotional share to 25%, three exits needing a vote) and "pass through in prices", despite worsening price perception. X is also more careful on the covenant: it counts no shrink gain in FY2026, warns that a third of last year's erosion wipes out the headroom, and plans to brief the lender early. Y handles all four trade-offs adequately but with less depth.

evidence.reasons: Both reproduce the key calculations correctly: the margin bridge, the gross-margin decomposition, $10.4M e-commerce drag, −$12.34 and −$1.64 per order, fee-test roll-out, and store exits of $6.6M, $4.4M and $2.2M. Both debunk the 6.1% claim and the "promotions work" correlation. X goes further: a wage-versus-productivity decomposition (+1.11 and −0.77 points), a reconciliation of 6.1% to −8.2%, break-even incrementality (94% for delivery, 39% for click-and-collect), low/base/high ranges per lever, and a sensitivity table with triggers. X's shrink clawback ($3.8–7.5M) is more measured than Y's $10M, which attributes the whole FY2023–25 shrink rise to hours, though Y flags it as an upper bound. Y books $2.3M of shrink gains in FY2026 and ignores lever interactions and promotion volume loss. X has a few shaky spots: the promotion break-even inference from cross-store comps, and several team allowances not in the pack. All are flagged as such.

revision.reasons: Both reject wage inflation as the main cause using the bridge (labour 13% of the decline). Both replace the 8% cut with a targeted ~3% reallocation that protects fresh and receiving hours, and both replace the e-commerce freeze with repricing. X is somewhat more thorough. It shows productivity offset two-thirds of the wage rise, tests the management view as an explicit condition ("not supported"), and projects the draft plan to FY2028 with the wage step included (1.1%). It also revises its own initial margin-first hypothesis when promotions and delivery alone prove insufficient. Y's revision is direct and correct, including the covenant implication of the draft plan, but less developed.

overall.reasons: The two documents share the same diagnosis and nearly the same seven levers, and Y is commendably concise and decision-ready. X would serve the CEO better in front of a board and lender. It builds the known wage and delivery-rate headwinds into the baseline and is honest that firm levers reach about 2.6%. It defines a sized second wave with a checkpoint trigger, and offers click-and-collect only as a fallback with the owners' commitment addressed. It also sizes the traffic risk and gives ranges and sensitivities. Y's 3.2% headline is more fragile, because it depends on excluding the wage rise and then leaning on stretch contingencies.
